slides.say: A printer finishes a job in sixty minutes. Its speed increases by twenty percent. How many minutes does the same job take now?
So the job stays the same, and only the speed changes. They ask for the new time.
at: They ask for the new time

slides.say: We'll solve it in two different ways. First by understanding, with the factor, like in the lesson. Then by plugging in numbers.
A twenty percent rise is one multiplier. Twenty percent more is a hundred twenty percent, so times one point two. And one point two is six fifths.
The job is the same, so the work is fixed. Like in the lesson, the speed and the time go opposite ways. So we flip the factor. Six fifths becomes five sixths.
Sixty times five sixths. Sixty divided by six is ten. Then ten times five is fifty minutes.
Does it make sense? Yes. Faster means less time, and fifty is less than sixty.
Careful with forty-eight, choice number one. Twenty percent of sixty is twelve. Then sixty minus twelve is forty-eight. But twenty percent faster doesn't mean twenty percent less time.
at: doesn't mean twenty percent less time

slides.say: So the job takes fifty minutes now. That's choice number two.
[pause] Now let's plug in numbers. We start again from the givens. The job size isn't given, so we choose it.
Let's say the job is three hundred pages. We pick three hundred because sixty divides it.
at: Let's say the job is three hundred pages

slides.say: Three hundred pages in sixty minutes. The rate is the work divided by the time. Three hundred divided by sixty is five pages a minute.
The speed increases by twenty percent. Twenty percent of five is one. So the new speed is five plus one, six pages a minute.
at: Twenty percent of five is one

slides.say: The job is still three hundred pages. So the time is the work divided by the new rate. Three hundred divided by six is fifty minutes. The same answer.
Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number two is our answer
